questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
nums = [10, 20, 30]
print(nums[3])
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
nums = [10, 20, 30]
print(nums[3])
```
questions.explanation_es: Los índices empiezan en 0, así que la última posición válida de una lista de tres elementos es 2. Pedir la 3 se sale del rango y Python lo dice en vez de devolver un valor vacío, que sería mucho peor de depurar.
questions.explanation_en: Indices start at 0, so the last valid position of a three-element list is 2. Asking for 3 is out of range, and Python says so rather than returning an empty value, which would be far worse to debug.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Common Sequence Operations

questions.question_es: ¿Qué operador comprueba si un valor está dentro de una lista?
questions.question_en: Which operator checks whether a value is inside a list?
questions.explanation_es: `3 in nums` devuelve un booleano recorriendo la lista. Es una búsqueda lineal: con colecciones grandes donde solo importa la pertenencia, un `set` responde en tiempo constante.
questions.explanation_en: `3 in nums` returns a boolean by scanning the list. It is a linear search: for large collections where only membership matters, a `set` answers in constant time.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Common Sequence Operations

questions.question_es: Una lista de Python puede contener elementos de tipos distintos a la vez.
questions.question_en: A Python list can hold elements of different types at the same time.
questions.explanation_es: `[1, "dos", 3.0, None]` es perfectamente válido: la lista guarda referencias a objetos, sin exigir un tipo común. Otra cosa es que convenga — mezclar tipos suele complicar el código que la consume.
questions.explanation_en: `[1, "two", 3.0, None]` is perfectly valid: a list stores references to objects without requiring a shared type. Whether it is wise is another matter — mixing types usually complicates the code consuming it.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Tutorial §3.1.3 (lists)

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
nums = [1, 2, 3]
nums[0] = 99
print(nums)
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
nums = [1, 2, 3]
nums[0] = 99
print(nums)
```
questions.explanation_es: Las listas son mutables: asignar a un índice **reemplaza** el elemento, no lo inserta. Para insertar sin perder nada está `insert(0, 99)`. Con un string la misma operación lanzaría `TypeError`.
questions.explanation_en: Lists are mutable: assigning to an index **replaces** the element, it does not insert. To insert without losing anything there is `insert(0, 99)`. On a string the same operation would raise `TypeError`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Tutorial §3.1.3 (lists)

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
print(list(range(3)) + [9])
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
print(list(range(3)) + [9])
```
questions.explanation_es: `range(3)` produce 0, 1 y 2 —el límite se excluye— y `+` concatena dos listas creando una tercera. Sumar una lista con un entero suelto, como `[0,1,2] + 9`, sí daría `TypeError`.
questions.explanation_en: `range(3)` yields 0, 1 and 2 — the stop value is excluded — and `+` concatenates two lists into a third. Adding a list to a bare integer, as in `[0,1,2] + 9`, would indeed raise `TypeError`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Functions: range() / list()

questions.question_es: ¿Cuál es la forma segura de leer el primer elemento de una lista que puede estar vacía?
questions.question_en: What is the safe way to read the first element of a list that may be empty?
questions.explanation_es: Las listas no tienen `.get()`: eso es de los diccionarios. Y `datos[0] or None` ya habría fallado al evaluar `datos[0]`. La expresión condicional comprueba primero que haya algo, aprovechando que la lista vacía es falsa.
questions.explanation_en: Lists have no `.get()`: that belongs to dictionaries. And `data[0] or None` would already have failed evaluating `data[0]`. The conditional expression checks there is something first, leaning on the empty list being falsy.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Truth Value Testing / Sequence Types

questions.question_es: Completa la función que devuelve el número de elementos de una lista: `___(nums)`
questions.question_en: Complete the function returning the number of elements in a list: `___(nums)`
questions.explanation_es: `len` es una función incorporada, no un método: se escribe `len(nums)` y no `nums.len()`. Funciona con cualquier secuencia y con diccionarios y conjuntos.
questions.explanation_en: `len` is a built-in function, not a method: you write `len(nums)` rather than `nums.len()`. It works with any sequence, and with dictionaries and sets too.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Functions: len()

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
nums = [1, 2, 3]
print(nums[-4] if len(nums) >= 4 else "fuera")
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
nums = [1, 2, 3]
print(nums[-4] if len(nums) >= 4 else "out")
```
questions.explanation_es: Los índices negativos también tienen límite: en una lista de 3 elementos van de −1 a −3, así que −4 se saldría. La condición corta antes de evaluar el acceso, que es justo para lo que sirve el ternario aquí.
questions.explanation_en: Negative indices have a limit too: in a three-element list they run from −1 to −3, so −4 would be out of range. The condition cuts in before the access is evaluated, which is exactly what the conditional expression is for here.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Common Sequence Operations

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
a = [1, 2]
a.append([3, 4])
print(len(a))
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
a = [1, 2]
a.append([3, 4])
print(len(a))
```
questions.explanation_es: `append` añade **un** elemento, y ese elemento es la lista entera: queda `[1, 2, [3, 4]]`, de largo 3. Para incorporar los elementos uno a uno está `extend`, que dejaría largo 4.
questions.explanation_en: `append` adds **one** element, and that element is the whole list: the result is `[1, 2, [3, 4]]`, of length 3. To fold the elements in one by one there is `extend`, which would give length 4.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Tutorial §5.1 (more on lists)

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
nums = [3, 1, 2]
ordenada = nums.sort()
print(ordenada)
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
nums = [3, 1, 2]
ordered = nums.sort()
print(ordered)
```
questions.explanation_es: `sort()` ordena la lista **en el sitio** y devuelve `None`, como casi todos los métodos que mutan. Quien quiere una lista nueva usa `sorted(nums)`. Este error deja la variable a `None` y el fallo aparece más tarde.
questions.explanation_en: `sort()` orders the list **in place** and returns `None`, like almost every mutating method. Anyone wanting a new list uses `sorted(nums)`. This mistake leaves the variable as `None`, and the failure shows up later.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: list.sort() / Built-in Functions: sorted()

questions.question_es: ¿Qué diferencia hay entre `pop()` y `remove()`?
questions.question_en: What is the difference between `pop()` and `remove()`?
options_es: `pop` borra todas las apariciones y `remove` solo la primera
`remove` devuelve el elemento borrado y `pop` no
`pop` quita por índice y devuelve el elemento; `remove` quita por valor y devuelve `None`
options_en: `pop` deletes every occurrence and `remove` only the first
`remove` returns the deleted element and `pop` does not
`pop` removes by index and returns the element; `remove` removes by value and returns `None`
questions.explanation_es: `pop()` sin argumento saca el último y te lo entrega, lo que permite usar la lista como pila. `remove(x)` busca el valor y borra solo la **primera** aparición; si no está, lanza `ValueError`.
questions.explanation_en: `pop()` with no argument takes the last one and hands it to you, which lets a list act as a stack. `remove(x)` searches for the value and deletes only the **first** occurrence; if it is absent, it raises `ValueError`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Tutorial §5.1 (more on lists)

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
nums = [1, 2, 3]
nums.extend("ab")
print(nums)
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
nums = [1, 2, 3]
nums.extend("ab")
print(nums)
```
questions.explanation_es: `extend` acepta cualquier iterable y un string itera carácter a carácter, así que entran dos elementos separados. Es una sorpresa frecuente: para añadir el string entero hay que usar `append`.
questions.explanation_en: `extend` accepts any iterable, and a string iterates character by character, so two separate elements go in. It is a frequent surprise: to add the whole string you need `append`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: list.extend()

questions.question_es: ¿Cómo se ordena una lista de strings por longitud?
questions.question_en: How do you sort a list of strings by length?
questions.explanation_es: `key` recibe una función que se aplica a cada elemento para obtener el valor por el que comparar. Se pasa la función sin llamarla: `key=len`, no `key=len()`. El orden es estable, así que las de igual longitud conservan su orden original.
questions.explanation_en: `key` takes a function applied to each element to obtain the value to compare by. The function is passed without calling it: `key=len`, not `key=len()`. The sort is stable, so equal-length items keep their original order.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Sorting HOW TO (key functions)

questions.question_es: `lista.index(x)` lanza `ValueError` si `x` no está en la lista.
questions.question_en: `items.index(x)` raises `ValueError` if `x` is not in the list.
questions.explanation_es: No devuelve −1 como en otros lenguajes: falla ruidosamente. Si la ausencia es un caso normal, conviene comprobar antes con `in` o envolverlo en `try`/`except ValueError`.
questions.explanation_en: It does not return −1 as in other languages: it fails loudly. If absence is a normal case, check first with `in` or wrap it in `try`/`except ValueError`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: list.index()

questions.question_es: Completa el método que cuenta cuántas veces aparece `2` en la lista: `nums.___(2)`
questions.question_en: Complete the method counting how many times `2` appears in the list: `nums.___(2)`
questions.explanation_es: `count` devuelve 0 si el valor no está, sin lanzar excepción — al revés que `index`. Recorre toda la lista, así que con datos grandes y muchas consultas conviene un `Counter`.
questions.explanation_en: `count` returns 0 when the value is absent, without raising — unlike `index`. It scans the whole list, so with large data and many lookups a `Counter` is the better tool.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: list.count()

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
nums = [1, 2, 3, 2]
nums.remove(2)
print(nums)
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
nums = [1, 2, 3, 2]
nums.remove(2)
print(nums)
```
questions.explanation_es: `remove` borra solo la **primera** coincidencia y deja las demás. Para eliminar todas hace falta un bucle o, más limpio, una comprensión: `[x for x in nums if x != 2]`.
questions.explanation_en: `remove` deletes only the **first** match and leaves the rest. To drop them all you need a loop or, more cleanly, a comprehension: `[x for x in nums if x != 2]`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: list.remove()

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
nums = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print(nums[::2])
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
nums = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print(nums[::2])
```
questions.explanation_es: El tercer valor es el paso: de dos en dos desde el principio, así que salen las posiciones 0, 2 y 4. Para empezar en la 1 habría que escribir `nums[1::2]`.
questions.explanation_en: The third value is the step: every two from the start, so positions 0, 2 and 4 come out. To begin at 1 you would write `nums[1::2]`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Common Sequence Operations (slicing) — https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#common-sequence-operations

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
nums = [1, 2, 3]
print(nums[10:20])
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
nums = [1, 2, 3]
print(nums[10:20])
```
questions.explanation_es: El slicing recorta a los límites reales en vez de fallar: si no queda nada, devuelve una lista vacía. Es lo contrario que el acceso por índice, que sí lanza `IndexError`, y por eso los slices son más tolerantes de lo que se espera.
questions.explanation_en: Slicing clamps to the real bounds instead of failing: if nothing is left, it returns an empty list. It is the opposite of index access, which does raise `IndexError`, and that is why slices are more forgiving than people expect.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Common Sequence Operations (slicing) — https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#common-sequence-operations

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
nums[1:3] = [9]
print(nums)
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
nums[1:3] = [9]
print(nums)
```
questions.explanation_es: Asignar a un slice sustituye ese tramo por los elementos del iterable, y **el largo puede cambiar**: aquí dos posiciones se reemplazan por una y la lista encoge. Se pueden borrar tramos enteros con `nums[1:3] = []`.
questions.explanation_en: Assigning to a slice replaces that stretch with the iterable's elements, and **the length may change**: here two positions are replaced by one and the list shrinks. Whole stretches can be deleted with `nums[1:3] = []`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Mutable Sequence Types

questions.question_es: ¿Qué tipo de copia hace `b = a[:]` sobre una lista de listas?
questions.question_en: What kind of copy does `b = a[:]` make of a list of lists?
options_es: Una copia superficial: la lista exterior es nueva, pero las interiores se comparten
Una copia profunda: los elementos también se duplican
Depende del tipo de los elementos
options_en: A shallow copy: the outer list is new, but the inner ones are shared
A deep copy: the elements are duplicated too
It depends on the element types
questions.explanation_es: Añadir a `b` no toca a `a`, pero mutar `b[0]` sí afecta a `a[0]`, porque ambas apuntan al mismo objeto interior. Para duplicar todos los niveles hace falta `copy.deepcopy`.
questions.explanation_en: Appending to `b` does not touch `a`, but mutating `b[0]` does affect `a[0]`, because both point at the same inner object. Duplicating every level requires `copy.deepcopy`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — copy — Shallow and deep copy operations

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
nums = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
print(nums[-2:])
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
nums = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
print(nums[-2:])
```
questions.explanation_es: `[-2:]` arranca dos posiciones antes del final y llega hasta el último: los dos últimos elementos. Es el idiom para «la cola» sin necesitar `len`.
questions.explanation_en: `[-2:]` starts two positions before the end and runs to the last: the final two elements. It is the idiom for 'the tail' without needing `len`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Common Sequence Operations (slicing) — https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#common-sequence-operations

questions.question_es: En `lista[inicio:fin]`, el elemento de la posición `fin` queda incluido en el resultado.
questions.question_en: In `items[start:stop]`, the element at position `stop` is included in the result.
questions.explanation_es: El final se excluye, igual que en `range`. Esa coherencia hace que `lista[:n] + lista[n:]` reconstruya la lista original sin repetir ni perder nada.
questions.explanation_en: The stop value is excluded, just as in `range`. That consistency is what makes `items[:n] + items[n:]` rebuild the original list without repeating or losing anything.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Tutorial §3.1.2 (slicing)

questions.question_es: Completa el slice que devuelve la lista invertida: `nums[___]`
questions.question_en: Complete the slice returning the reversed list: `nums[___]`
questions.explanation_es: Sin inicio ni fin y con paso −1 recorre toda la secuencia hacia atrás, devolviendo una copia nueva. `reversed(nums)` hace lo mismo sin copiar, devolviendo un iterador.
questions.explanation_en: With no start or stop and a step of −1 it walks the whole sequence backwards, returning a fresh copy. `reversed(nums)` does the same without copying, returning an iterator.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Common Sequence Operations (slicing) — https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#common-sequence-operations

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
nums = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print(nums[4:1:-1])
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
nums = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print(nums[4:1:-1])
```
questions.explanation_es: Con paso negativo se empieza en 4 y se baja excluyendo la posición 1: salen 4, 3 y 2. La regla de excluir el final se mantiene también al ir hacia atrás, que es lo que suele descolocar.
questions.explanation_en: With a negative step it starts at 4 and counts down, excluding position 1: 4, 3 and 2 come out. The rule of excluding the stop holds when going backwards too, which is what usually throws people.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Common Sequence Operations (slicing) — https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#common-sequence-operations

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
filas = [[0] * 2] * 2
filas[0][0] = 9
print(filas)
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
rows = [[0] * 2] * 2
rows[0][0] = 9
print(rows)
```
questions.explanation_es: `* 2` sobre la lista exterior no copia la interior: repite **la misma referencia** dos veces, así que ambas filas son el mismo objeto. La forma correcta es una comprensión: `[[0] * 2 for _ in range(2)]`, que crea una lista nueva por fila.
questions.explanation_en: `* 2` on the outer list does not copy the inner one: it repeats **the same reference** twice, so both rows are the same object. The correct way is a comprehension: `[[0] * 2 for _ in range(2)]`, which builds a fresh list per row.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Programming FAQ (how do I create a multidimensional list)

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
m = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
print(m[1][0])
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
m = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
print(m[1][0])
```
questions.explanation_es: El primer índice elige la fila y el segundo la columna: fila 1 es `[3, 4]` y su posición 0 es 3. Invertir el orden mentalmente —`m[0][1]`, que da 2— es el error más común al empezar con matrices.
questions.explanation_en: The first index picks the row and the second the column: row 1 is `[3, 4]` and its position 0 is 3. Flipping the order mentally — `m[0][1]`, which gives 2 — is the commonest slip when starting with matrices.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Tutorial §5.1.4 (nested list comprehensions)

questions.question_es: ¿Cómo se transpone una matriz `m = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]` de forma idiomática?
questions.question_en: How do you transpose a matrix `m = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]` idiomatically?
questions.explanation_es: `*m` desempaqueta las filas como argumentos y `zip` las empareja por columnas. `m[::-1]` solo invierte el orden de las filas y `transpose` no existe en las listas — es de NumPy.
questions.explanation_en: `*m` unpacks the rows as arguments and `zip` pairs them column-wise. `m[::-1]` merely reverses the row order, and `transpose` does not exist on lists — it belongs to NumPy.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Tutorial §5.1.4 (nested list comprehensions) / zip()

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
m = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
print(len(m), len(m[0]))
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
m = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
print(len(m), len(m[0]))
```
questions.explanation_es: `len(m)` cuenta las filas y `len(m[0])` los elementos de la primera. Ojo: nada garantiza que todas las filas midan lo mismo, porque una lista anidada no obliga a ser rectangular.
questions.explanation_en: `len(m)` counts the rows and `len(m[0])` the elements of the first one. Note that nothing guarantees every row is the same length, because a nested list is under no obligation to be rectangular.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Functions: len()

questions.question_es: `copy.deepcopy(matriz)` es necesario para duplicar una lista anidada sin que las filas queden compartidas.
questions.question_en: `copy.deepcopy(matrix)` is needed to duplicate a nested list without the rows staying shared.
questions.explanation_es: `matriz[:]`, `list(matriz)` y `matriz.copy()` copian solo el nivel exterior y dejan las filas compartidas. `deepcopy` recorre la estructura entera. Para una matriz sencilla también sirve `[fila[:] for fila in matriz]`, más rápido.
questions.explanation_en: `matrix[:]`, `list(matrix)` and `matrix.copy()` copy only the outer level and leave the rows shared. `deepcopy` walks the whole structure. For a simple matrix `[row[:] for row in matrix]` also works, and is faster.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — copy — Shallow and deep copy operations

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?

```python
m = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
print(sum(sum(fila) for fila in m))
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?

```python
m = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
print(sum(sum(row) for row in m))
```
questions.explanation_es: El `sum` interior suma cada fila (3 y 7) y el exterior suma esos totales: 10. Aplicar `sum(m)` directamente fallaría, porque intentaría sumar listas a un entero.
questions.explanation_en: The inner `sum` adds each row (3 and 7) and the outer one adds those totals: 10. Applying `sum(m)` directly would fail, since it would try to add lists to an integer.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Functions: sum()

questions.question_es: Completa la comprensión que crea una matriz 2x3 de ceros sin filas compartidas: `[[0] * 3 ___ _ in range(2)]`
questions.question_en: Complete the comprehension creating a 2x3 matrix of zeros with no shared rows: `[[0] * 3 ___ _ in range(2)]`
questions.explanation_es: La comprensión ejecuta `[0] * 3` en cada vuelta, así que cada fila es una lista nueva. El guion bajo es la convención para una variable de bucle que no se usa.
questions.explanation_en: The comprehension runs `[0] * 3` on each pass, so every row is a fresh list. The underscore is the convention for a loop variable that goes unused.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Programming FAQ (how do I create a multidimensional list)

questions.question_es: ¿Por qué `[[0] * 3] * 2` falla como matriz pero `[0] * 3` funciona como fila?
questions.question_en: Why does `[[0] * 3] * 2` fail as a matrix while `[0] * 3` works as a row?
options_es: Porque `0` es inmutable y compartirlo no se nota; la lista interior es mutable y sí
Porque la segunda dimensión debe declararse antes
Porque `0` no puede repetirse más de tres veces
options_en: Because `0` is immutable and sharing it is invisible; the inner list is mutable and shows
Because the second dimension must be declared first
Because `0` cannot be repeated more than three times
Because `*` does not accept nested lists
questions.explanation_es: En ambos casos `*` repite referencias. Con enteros no importa: reasignar `fila[0] = 9` sustituye la referencia en esa posición y no toca a las demás. Con listas, mutar el objeto compartido se ve desde todas las filas.
questions.explanation_en: In both cases `*` repeats references. With integers it does not matter: reassigning `row[0] = 9` replaces the reference at that position and leaves the others alone. With lists, mutating the shared object is visible from every row.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Programming FAQ (how do I create a multidimensional list)
